title: Benchmark harness: thread/thermal/jitter probing
content:
Summary:
This is a working note describing a throughput benchmarking harness variant that focuses on: thread scheduling and affinity, thermal/temperature conditioning effects on GPU throughput, and end-to-end jitter characterization. The goal is to identify subtle non-deterministic throughput regressions that only appear under long-run thermal drift, thread preemption, or small microburst mixes.

Why this is different:
- Existing harnesses deliberately target steady throughput and warmup behavior; this doc explores cross-cutting sources of variance (OS scheduler, GPU thermal throttling, driver-level resets, power-capping) and prescribes reproducible experiments to surface them.

Objectives:
1) Produce a repeatable experiment and capture-format to detect throughput degradation driven by thermal drift or thread preemption.
2) Define a small set of loadgen configs that exercise microbursts, co-located lower-priority workloads, and single-tenant isolation cases.
3) Provide an operational checklist for conditioning hardware and collecting low-level telemetry to triage regressions.

Assumptions / scope:
- Targeted at GPU-backed inference hosts used by Redwood Dedicated and Private.
- Focus on transformer-based decoder-only models with long KV cache usage patterns (typical token lengths 8-256).
- Not covering multi-node RDMA scaling in this iteration.

Metrics to collect (primary):
- tokens_per_second (host-level aggregate)
- p50/p95/p99 latency (ms) per request
- request_success_rate (%) and error taxonomy (OOM, NVML driver errors, gRPC timeouts)
- GPU SM utilization, power draw (W), GPU temperature (C), GPU clocks (MHz), memory utilization (MiB)
- CPU steal, context-switch rate, runqueue length, irq/softirq rates on critical cores
- Kernel-level counters where available: scheduler preemptions, process migrations

Measurement matrix (csv logging fields):
- run_id, timestamp_utc, config_profile, target_qps, mean_latency_ms, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, tps, gpu_temp_c, gpu_power_w, sm_util_pct, cpu_load_pct, errors, notes

Baseline conditioning protocol (to reduce noise):
1) Reboot node or start from freshly idle system image to remove residual thermal state.
2) Ensure nvidia-persistenced is running and NVML reports stable clocks.
3) Set governor to performance where available (nvidia-smi -ac if allowed).
4) Clear page cache and restart serving runtime to ensure clean kernel pages.
5) Wait 5 minutes at idle to allow GPU to return to baseline temperature (record baseline temp).

Thermal drift experiment sequence (30--120 minute runs):
- Phase A (priming): 5 minutes of ramped traffic at 20% of target QPS to populate KV cache and JITed kernels.
- Phase B (stress): 60 min at sustained target QPS with 10% periodic microbursts (+200% QPS for 5s every 60s).
- Phase C (cooldown injection): introduce low-priority co-located workload for 20 minutes (synthetic GPU worker) to simulate noisy neighbor.
- Phase D (recovery probe): drop to 10% QPS and measure latency and error recovery for 5 minutes.
Record telemetry continuously and capture timestamped snapshots from NVML and /proc for correlation.

Loadgen config examples (YAML-like, plain text):
- config: baseline-steady
  description: 10m warmup then 20m steady at target
  target_qps: 500
  request_shape: {tokens: 64, batch: 1}
  microburst: null

- config: microburst-oscillate
  description: periodic 5s bursts to surface scheduling jitter
  target_qps: 400
  microburst: {burst_qps: 1200, burst_duration_s: 5, period_s: 60}
  priming: {duration_s: 300, qps: 0.2 * target_qps}

- config: co-located-noise
  description: background GPU worker launched on same host to simulate contention
  target_qps: 450
  noise_worker: {type: matmul, devices: [0], intensity: 0.25}

Repeatability rules (critical):
- Use deterministic request corpus seeded by a stable RNG seed. Store the seed with run metadata.
- Fix entropy sources: disable system cron jobs, network scans, and any automatic updates during runs.
- Pin loadgen client and server processes to CPU cores with explicit affinity (taskset) and document the mappings. Do not rely on default scheduler placement.
- Use identical model version and quantization artifact hashes for each run. Keep a checksum in metadata.
- Maintain identical runtime flags: batching windows, max-concurrent-requests, kv-cache policy.

Thread affinity and NUMA guidance:
- Pin serving runtime worker threads that handle GPU submission to a small core set adjacent to PCIe root. Example affinity map:
  - gpu0_submit_threads -> cores 8-11 (isolated cpuset)
  - admin/observer daemons -> cores 0-3
  - loadgen client -> remote machine when possible; if co-located, pin to cores 12-15
- For multi-socket hosts, make sure GPU-to-CPU NUMA affinity is respected (numactl --physcpubind).

Profiling hooks and low-level telemetry (what to collect):
- NVML: temperature, power, clocks, utilization every 5s.
- nvidia-smi topo -m before run and at the end to detect PCIe changes.
- perf: per-process cycles and context-switch counters sampled every minute.
- dmesg / kernel log tail: capture driver resets, TDR-like messages.
- traces: brief 10s perf record + nvprof snapshot at first sign of degradation for correlation.

Failure modes and triage signals:
- Gradual TPS decline with rising GPU temp -> likely thermal throttling or power capping. Check nvml clocks and power.
- Abrupt latency spike coincident with CPU runqueue growth -> OS preemption. Look at irq/softirq and context-switches.
- Increasing p99 with stable mean -> tail-latency induced by garbage collection or background compaction.
- Repeated NVML errors or driver disconnects -> escalate to infra/driver team; capture nvidia-bug-report.

A reproducible run checklist for engineers:
- [ ] Verify model checksum and runtime flags in metadata file.
- [ ] Reboot or reset node; confirm baseline GPU temp recorded.
- [ ] Start telemetry collectors (nvml_exporter, node_exporter, perf recorder).
- [ ] Start loadgen with explicit seed and affinity mapping.
- [ ] Monitor for >10% deviation vs baseline TPS in first 10 minutes; abort early if driver errors.
- [ ] At end, collect nvidia-smi -q, dmesg, /var/log/syslog, and serving runtime logs.

Result logging and example row:
run-2025-01-10T09:12,2025-01-10T09:12:15Z,microburst-oscillate,400,8.9,7.1,23.2,45.8,4200,78,220,85,0,"notes: temp rose 6C during interval"

Operational notes / gotchas:
- Cloud VMs may have host-level power capping that is opaque; validate with infra whether power limits are enforced by hypervisor.
- Driver versions matter: a small NVML change can change the way clocks are reported — include driver version in metadata.
- Preemption from monitoring agents (e.g., live reallocation) has caused flapping in past runs; consider a maintenance window.

Open questions and next steps:
- Should we add a synthetic thermal chamber (fan control) to force a very repeatable thermal curve across runs? Pros: deterministic thermal ramp. Cons: operationally heavy.
- Evaluate if low-frequency perf sampling (1m resolution) is sufficient, or whether we need per-second counters for context switches.
- Create a canonical CSV/archival format and an ingestion pipeline into Confluence/benchmark DB for historical comparisons.

Appendix: quick run commands (examples)
- Start telemetry exporter: nohup nvml_collector --interval 5 --out /tmp/nvml_run.csv &
- Launch loadgen with seed: ./loadgen --profile microburst-oscillate --seed 1337 --affinity map.json --out /tmp/run-logs &
- Snapshot commands at end: nvidia-smi -q > nvidia_q_end.txt; dmesg -T | tail -n 200 > dmesg_end.txt

If this experiment surfaces a reproducible regression, include the full run-id and attach the raw telemetry. We will iterate on the noise-injection patterns and consider adding a variation that runs the same sequence under different driver and kernel versions to isolate root causes.
